item.title: Time in Entrepreneurship: New Perspectives and Approaches
item.content:encoded:
Ludvig Levasseur, Indian Institute of Management Bangalore

Moren Lévesque, York University

Paul Spee, University of Queensland

Ute Stephan, King's College London

Matthew Wood, University of Oklahoma

This special issue seeks manuscripts advancing our understanding of time in entrepreneurship. Research on the duration, pace, timing, and speed of action calibration in entrepreneurial processes such as opportunity realization are key examples of the role temporal dynamics play in entrepreneurship. Time is equally critical when examining decisions about the timing of growth while managing external events and shocks alongside slowly or rapidly evolving industry trends and customer preferences. Further lines of inquiry concern the pace, timing, and speed of exit decisions, or decisions to pursue venturing activities over time. Entrepreneurs' subjective perceptions of time, and their own and their stakeholders' orientations towards the short- vs. long-term, the past, present or future shape how they navigate entrepreneurship.

Nearly three decades have passed since the first (and only) ETP special issue on time in entrepreneurship (Bird & West, 1997). Yet, scholars continually advocate that we should pay more attention to time in entrepreneurship and there is a growing body of work on time in management, in strategy, and in organizational behavior. This suggests a need for entrepreneurship scholarship to learn from how time is discussed in other disciplines and to engage more deeply with the study of the specifics of time and temporality in entrepreneurship, accounting for unique temporal challenges entrepreneurs must navigate in their daily activities. Despite the pervasive influence of time itself as a target for action across academia and industry, we lack a dedicated conversation on time as the main focus for theory development, extension, and testing in entrepreneurship.

More than simply the passing of time as a background condition, time itself is a multilevel phenomenon across levels of analyses from the individual entrepreneur and teams to entrepreneurial firms and societies. The editors are especially interested in work that addresses the subjective elements of time—how time is experienced, shaped, and communicated—and how the subjective elements might flow from objective temporal artifacts (clock time, schedules, deadlines, etc.). There is limited understanding of how entrepreneurs engage in temporal manipulation and time as sense-making and sense-giving such that subjective experience of time diverges from objective time to, for instance, create a sense of fleeting investment opportunity.

The subjective aspects of time are critical, raising questions about the effects of interpretations or manipulations of time on outcomes like entrepreneurial orientation, preparedness in pitch presentation, and investor decisions to provide funding. There is limited understanding of how temporal dimensions—duration, pace, timing, speed, and related windows of opportunity—impact the creation, running, and managing of new ventures. There is a lack of clear comprehension of how these dimensions may shape not only venture outcomes but also the psychology of entrepreneurs including their motivations, efforts, sense of progress, well-being, physical and mental health, and how they relate to stakeholders.

The editors seek research to examine how temporal dimensions impact entrepreneurs, their stakeholders, and ventures. Importantly, research should be more than simply processual, longitudinal, and historical. While processual, longitudinal, and historical approaches are welcomed, the phenomena of time should be central/core rather than peripheral. Simply looking at how a phenomenon unfolds over time is insufficient for inclusion in the special issue. The editors look for studies that focus on theorizing and investigating the role of time, addressing how entrepreneurs' temporally oriented practices and actions impact entrepreneurial processes and outcomes.

Looking at these practices and actions over time illuminates the role and influence of time, which strengthens entrepreneurship as the focal context as entrepreneurs and new ventures navigate unique temporal challenges such as liability of newness, absence of legitimacy, and uncertainty. Simulation studies have promise, allowing investigations of the influence of engagement with time itself as driver of thinking, action, and outcomes, over longer periods than empirical work can typically sustain. Providing a deeper understanding of the role of subjective time could also be done in relation to entrepreneurs' actions, ventures, and their strategies, and how these relationships are shaped by macro-level contexts such as industries, and how communities, regions, and countries are impacted by institutional, religious, and cultural contexts.

Research could bring new insights into how macro-level conditions, events, shocks, and crises, and other external enablers or disablers impact how entrepreneurs and their ventures navigate time. Moreover, both objective and subjective time may help explain heterogeneity and inclusion in entrepreneurship, decolonization, and sustainability and social impact outcomes of entrepreneurship.

The editors invite interested scholars to submit cutting-edge manuscripts that seek to advance theoretical and empirical understanding and knowledge of the role and influence of time in entrepreneurship beyond what is already known, and across levels of analysis and contexts. Manuscripts may draw on knowledge from other fields and disciplines, and generate time-based theorizing that is unique to entrepreneurship. The editors value manuscripts that employ or triangulate different methodological approaches to analyze time in entrepreneurship such as controlled or natural experiments, simulations, formal modelling, machine learning approaches and diverse qualitative research approaches. The editors seek the next generation of rigorous and impactful (theoretical and empirical) research with the core focus on time, and expect manuscripts to make significant novel (theoretical, empirical, and/or methodological) contributions to entrepreneurship literature.

Potential topics

  • How do objective dimensions such as duration, pace, timing, speed, and window of opportunity impact the entrepreneurship process?
  • How do they shape links between entrepreneurs' subjective time perspective, their biological time (chronotype), and cognitive processes related to information scanning and learning?
  • How do entrepreneurs' subjective time perspectives relate to their cognitions including information scanning and search, entrepreneurial learning, information associations and connections, and opportunity evaluation and judgment?
  • How do time perspectives relate to informal investors' and venture capitalists' decision to provide funding?
  • How do investors' time perspectives shape who they invest in, and the timing and size of their investments?
  • With what pace and speed do failure consequences vary with institutional and cultural contexts?
  • How does the timing of these consequences vary across groups of entrepreneurs including minoritized groups and differently abled entrepreneurs?
  • When and how does time perspective lead to unhealthy persistence in entrepreneurship and undermine well-being?
  • How do entrepreneurs' perception of time and the temporal development of the business impact venture emergence, business sustainability, and social entrepreneurship?
  • Do we see variations in temporal profiles and differences across industries and cultures?
  • How do the pacing of external events and entrepreneurs' own time perspective relate to how they manage equity, diversity, decolonization, and inclusion within their ventures?

Timeline

  • September 30, 2027: Submission deadline
